events.lage: Past midnight you go up for air. Holm hasn't gone to bed. She is sitting on the foredeck with the case open across a hatch cover, and inside lies a double rifle with two worn barrels and a dark walnut stock. She got it up here by herself, and you can see what that cost her.

zeilen.text: This has been in my family longer than this ship has floated, so I don't give it away. But it can't stand on a quay by itself, and I can't hold it through a fight. Not by the twenty-first.

So I lend it to the best shot on this coast, and I don't know who that is yet. Adrien up at the bergerie, your dead deserter, thinks he knows. Elsa is sure she knows. And I have called a sergeant who doesn't care what anyone thinks.
So I lend it to the best shot on this coast, and I don't know who that is yet. Rosi thinks she knows. Elsa is sure she knows. And I have called a sergeant who doesn't care what anyone thinks.
Beat all three on my foredeck and you carry it on the twenty-first. Then you bring it back.

optionen.text: Runs a hand along the barrels. “When?”

zeile.text: Any evening, when the light goes. I'm not going anywhere, the doctors made sure of that.

events.lage: The last echo goes out over the water. Holm takes the rifle from you and raises it with her good arm. She shoots once, and the last bottle out on the water is gone. Then she sits down, a little too fast. She breaks the rifle open and holds it out to you. Her other hand has gone back to her side.

zeilen.text: You beat all three. You have not beaten me. Ask me again when the fighting is over.
It pulls left. Everyone in my family does.

optionen.text: Takes Gemelli, Holm's double rifle, with both hands.

zeile.text: Bring it back, Frankfurt.

events.lage: Adrien, the soldier Wolff wrote down as dead, has come down from the bergerie in a borrowed shirt, and nobody on board asks his name. Holm has put a box of cartridges on a hatch cover and a row of bottles out on the water.

zeilen.text: Laetitia says I can't shoot with this shoulder. I told her I only need one good one. You have two, which seems unfair.
Three rounds, and most hits after three wins. You get five seconds between rounds, and you load your own rifle.
No wind tonight, so you have no excuse. And leave my gulls alone, it costs you a hit.

optionen.text: Takes the rifle.

zeile.text: After you. I'm dead, I can wait.

events.lage: Rosi comes up from the engine room with grease on her arms and her own ear defenders. She looks the rifle over the way she looks at every machine, and she likes it more than she likes you.

zeilen.text: Whoever made these barrels knew the job. Now watch me ruin your evening, Officer.
Three rounds, and most hits after three wins. You get five seconds between rounds, and you load your own rifle.
No wind tonight, so you have no excuse. And leave my gulls alone, it costs you a hit.

optionen.text: “Loser cleans the bilge.”

zeile.text: Deal. And it goes on the whiteboard in my workshop, Officer.

events.lage: Elsa Ferrandi comes aboard out of uniform. She still stands like she is wearing it. She checks the rifle twice, then she checks your hands.

zeilen.text: I'm here as a private person, First Officer. A private person with eleven years of range scores. Holm says all of this is legal, and I'd like to keep believing her.

The wind is up tonight, so aim against it. And one of my gulls stole a flash grenade from our stores and keeps coming back. Hit the grenade, not the bird, and the other shooter sees nothing for five seconds.

optionen.text: “Any advice?”

zeile.text: Yes. Keep the barrels away from the gendarmerie.

events.lage: A grey Legion jeep stops on the quay at dusk. Sergent Wolff, the Legion man from the Genoese tower, comes up the gangway with a notebook and a sharp pencil, and he salutes Holm properly. She doesn't salute back, she shakes his hand. Neither of them says anything about her side.

zeilen.text: Who is that man at the rail? He looks like a caporal of mine. A good man and a terrible shot. He died on a mountain. It was in my report.
You lied to me and took my deserter out by sea, Officer. Tonight I'm off duty, so I will only beat you.
You gave me my man and you did it by the book, Officer. So I will beat you politely.
Captain Holm tells me you can shoot, Officer. I'll need to see that for myself.
I read about him. Sad story. They say his sergeant wrote it very well.
It was the best thing that man ever wrote, and he didn't do it to be thanked.
No. But if I ever meet him, I'll buy him a drink. And then I'll let him win.
You could not stop him. Now go and stand somewhere else, whoever you are.

optionen.text: “Write this one down, then.”

zeile.text: I always do. Begin.

events.lage: Holm is on the foredeck when the light goes, with a crate of bottles and a small tin box. She still moves like someone carrying a very full glass. She has the cartridges for Gemelli, her double rifle, lined up on the hatch cover, and she has counted them.

zeilen.text: You beat three people who were not me. The stitches still pull, so this is your chance, Frankfurt.
One round, one gift. That's how my father taught me. Every round you win, the box gets lighter.

optionen.text: Looks into the tin box.

zeile.text: Steel, a stone and a bar of copper. Rosi will know what to do. Now shoot.

zeilen.text: Two good shoulders. I told you it was unfair.
A dead man just beat you. Please don't put that in a report.

optionen.text: Nods.

zeilen.text: Fine, one line on the whiteboard for you, but only one.
That's another line for me, Officer. I'm running out of board.

optionen.text: Nods.

zeilen.text: Not bad. I'll pretend I didn't see how you hold it.
Again, First Officer. Slower hands. That's not advice, it's a complaint.

optionen.text: Nods.

zeilen.text: Noted. You shot better than me tonight. I don't write that often.
I wrote down all your misses. Would you like the list?

optionen.text: Nods.

zeilen.text: That's the first time. Stitches or not, I will remember it.
Again, Frankfurt. The box isn't empty.
Steel. Give it to Rosi, then she'll be nice to you for an hour.
Aquamarine, for the sabre. Yes, I know about the sabre.
Copper. My father kept that for Gemelli and never used it. Now it's your turn to carry the guilt.

optionen.text: Nods.

events.lage: Holm reloads without looking at you.

zeilen.text: Again, Frankfurt.

optionen.text: Reloads.

events.lage: The barrel is nearly empty when Madame Casanova climbs on a crate for one more speech, mostly to the boats. At the end she stops, lifts her chin and waits. She always leaves this pause, for the applause. Nobody in the harbour claps. Then somebody does: a thin man behind the barrel, in a double-breasted pinstripe suit and a white fedora, clapping carefully so he doesn't spill his glass. There is barrel dirt on one knee of the suit. A folded list sticks out of his breast pocket, in beautiful upright handwriting, like a wedding invitation.

zeilen.text: Somebody has to, or she starts again. Pascal Leca, deputy mayor. If a thing in this town doesn't need a speech, it's probably me.
And you're Duc. Yes, I asked. You could have stayed on your boat tonight, and nobody here would have blamed you. You didn't. This village will remember that, Duc, and so will I.
Now, you're bleeding on my harbour. That's not a complaint. Here, take these, the pharmacy doesn't open until Thursday.

The Lieutenant has her list of the damage, and at the top of it I've written that the crew of the Eden Rise defended the quay. So nobody will send you a bill. Anything you need while you're stuck here, you come to me first. Leave it with me.

optionen.text: Takes the bandages and shakes his hand. “Thanks, Pascal.”

zeile.text: No, no, you have it the wrong way round. We owe you. People here count what they owe, Duc. It's the one thing we're good at.

optionen.text: Looks at the suit, then at the barrel. “You rolled that thing in that suit?”

zeile.text: I know. My tailor in Bastia is going to cry. But a man with no hair has to look good somewhere, Duc, and I've run out of other places.

optionen.text: “Where were you when the boar came?”

zeile.text: Up in the church tower, ringing the bell. Badly. The priest was, let's say, praying. I had never rung a bell in my life, and now the whole town knows it.

optionen.text: “So you're the one who really runs this place.”

zeile.text: Shh, please. She has very good ears for that. I carry the broom, Duc. That's all I do, I carry the broom.

events.lage: An old Vespa comes down the harbour steps. Not the road, the steps. It stops with the front wheel ten centimetres from your shoe. On it sits a young woman in a pink rain jacket and a pink helmet, already holding out a handful of envelopes.

zeilen.text: You're the yacht! Hi, Yacht! Three bills, one letter from a bank and one love letter. No, I don't read them. I just know. Love letters are always on the good paper.
These ones are from Monaco, that's your boss, yes? Funny, the deputy mayor gets more post from Monaco than you do. And he writes back like it's to the Pope, every letter perfect. It must be the hat.
Mina Orsoni. Those are stairs. I have told you what stairs are. Thirty euros.
Not agaaaain! Elsa, I was going slowly, I was only going slowly downwards!

optionen.text: Looks at the wheel, then at his shoe. “You nearly killed me.”

zeile.text: Nearly! Ask anybody, I've never hit a person. Two goats and a priest, but the priest was standing in the road.

optionen.text: Holds out five euros. “Who's the love letter for?”

zeile.text: Five euros says it isn't for you. Ten euros says I saw nothing, and I'm very expensive when I see nothing.

optionen.text: “Elsa, let me pay it. She brought my post.”

zeile.text: You can't, First Officer. She would only do it again, and then I'd have to be nice to you as well.

optionen.text: “Slow down, kid.”

zeile.text: Kid? I'm twenty-four! I have a licence and everything. Well. I have a licence.

events.lage: Video call from the town hall. Pascal is at his desk, standing up, eating a sandwich over a stack of paper. His hat hangs on the corner of the old mayor's portrait.

zeilen.text: Duc, sorry, one minute only. I ring the hospital in Ajaccio every morning, they know me there now, and your captain has just thrown a yoghurt at a doctor. I thought you'd want to know. I think it's a very good sign.
I told her the boat is in good hands, because nobody else had. She said something in Norwegian. I wrote it down, in case it was medical.

optionen.text: “You don't have to do this, you know.”

zeile.text: I know. That's why it's nice. You held my quay, Duc. I can hold a telephone.

optionen.text: “What did she say?”

zeile.text: I have it here. T, A, K, K. The nurse says it means thank you. Then she threw the yoghurt, though, so I don't know.

optionen.text: “Tell her Frankfurt says get well.”

zeile.text: Frankfurt. I will. I'll say it exactly like that, and I'll stand well back.

events.lage: The harbourmaster has found you on the quay. He is a lovely man with a folder, and this is minute eleven. You have heard about his cousin in Propriano, and now he is on the third page of what you owe. Then a paper cup of coffee appears in your hand, and a white fedora appears beside it.

zeilen.text: Toussaint, your wife rang, the fish is getting cold. And think about it, my friend. The Eden Rise can't move, so it isn't a boat, it's a building. Buildings don't pay mooring fees.
Look at that, he's gone. Here's what you paid him already, Duc, he had it in the folder. Drink that, you look like you slept on a rope. It's the least we can do, after the quay.

optionen.text: Raises the paper cup. “I owe you one.”

zeile.text: You don't, and you won't. I keep very good accounts, Duc, and you are a long way ahead.

optionen.text: “What do you get out of all this, Pascal?”

zeile.text: Do you know, nobody has ever asked me that. A village that is still here in ten years, I suppose. And a chair at Alva's, if I ever get the time to sit down.

optionen.text: Sniffs the cup. “What's in this?”

zeile.text: Coffee and a small prayer. It's from Alva's, so it's mostly the prayer.

betroffen.was: has a biscuit in each hand

events.lage: Lola comes down the town hall steps with red eyes and a huge grin, and Jana comes down behind her, holding a biscuit in each hand. It turns out the town hall has an old telephone with a real wire. The deputy mayor left it on his desk with a plate of biscuits, and then he went out for an hour.

zeilen.text: Boss, that man! He asked me what Nan's name was before I'd even sat down! I was on for an hour and ten and she didn't ring the coast guard once!
He says Mama can ring back on it, Sir, any Sunday, and it's free because of you. Because of the quay. I don't know what to do. Sorry. Should I write him a letter?

optionen.text: “Write him a letter.”

zeile.text: Okay! Yes! Lola, how do you spell grateful?

optionen.text: Takes one of Jana's biscuits. “Nobody has ever left me biscuits.”

zeile.text: Mate, get in line. I looked in all his drawers for more. They're locked.

events.lage: Pascal finds you outside Alva's, a list in one hand and a small wooden box in the other. Word has gone round that the Ricci brothers have stopped working the harbour, and that their big cousin is walking strangely.

zeilen.text: Duc. Eleven purses this summer, one wedding ring and Petru's tobacco, and the tobacco was the one that frightened me. And now, nothing, for days. People are leaving their bags on the chairs again.
The town can't pay you, you've seen the town. But this has been in the safe since before my time. A Genoese captain left it to settle a bar bill, and all it has ever done is sit there.
Your engineer says she can put it in that bat of yours. I didn't understand one word she said, I just nodded. Please take it. It's a small thing, for what this village owes you.

optionen.text: Opens the box. A green stone, cool in the hand. “Pascal, this is worth real money.”

zeile.text: Probably. Don't tell Madame, she'd make it into a fountain.

optionen.text: “It was three idiots with a bag.”

zeile.text: To you, Duc. To Madame Paoli it was her husband's ring, and he has been dead nine years. She got it back on Tuesday. She wants to feed you.

optionen.text: “Tell them they're welcome.”

zeile.text: Tell them yourself. They keep buying you drinks at Alva's, and you keep not being there. Petru has drunk three of them for you.

events.lage: You can't sleep, so you walk up through the village at five in the morning. The piazza is dark. At the top of the town hall steps Madame Casanova stands in a dressing gown and rubber boots, holding a stack of cards. Her only audience is Kevin, on the edge of the fountain.

zeilen.text: People of Cala d'Orsu. No. Friends. In this, our hour of… no. Kevin, you are not even trying.
Monsieur. You saw nothing. This is a mayor inspecting her steps.
My father built these, you know. He could fill this square just by coming out to buy cigarettes. I need a cannon.

optionen.text: Sits down on the cold step. “Read me the one you're working on.”

zeile.text: It's very short. “Thank you for coming.” That is all of it. I have been trying to give that speech for years, Monsieur, and I always add something.

optionen.text: Claps slowly, alone, in the dark.

zeile.text: Oh, don't. Pascal does that. He thinks I don't know that he's the only one.

optionen.text: Says nothing and walks on, so she can keep going.

zeile.text: People of Cala d'Orsu. Kevin, one more time.

events.lage: Madame Casanova has come aboard with a sash, a photographer and a chart of the bay. Megan is here for one night and has no time for any of it. Four minutes later they are bent over the same chart, and neither of them wants to be the first to say she is enjoying herself.

zeilen.text: Here, the yacht, every light on! Here, the cannon! Madame, when it fires, every telephone in Corsica will point at this bay!
Every telephone in Corsica. Go on. I have investors who like a nice view, mind. Could your people stand a wee bit further to the left?
Madame! My people are the view!
You would do very well in my business. That's not a compliment, it's a warning.

optionen.text: “The village stays in the picture.”

zeile.text: Monsieur! Write that down! No, I will write it down, you would leave out the adjectives.

optionen.text: “The investors are paying for the fuel.”

zeile.text: Thank you, First Officer. Somebody on this boat can count.

optionen.text: Puts a glass on the chart. “Stand the investors on the quay with everybody else, and give them a drink.”

zeile.text: Aye. All right. That's actually not terrible. Don't tell her I said so.

events.lage: When you come out, Pascal is standing in the corridor with his hat in his hands, as if he had only just arrived. He doesn't ask what she said. He gives you a canvas bag: bandages, a flask of coffee, and a sandwich wrapped in the town's official paper.

zeilen.text: You're going up, then. I thought you would. I told the priest to stay down here, and he listened to me. I'm glad you are not that kind of man.
Bring yourself back, Duc. I mean it, we've only just got you. This village owes you enough already, and I don't want to owe you more.

optionen.text: Takes the bag. “Keep the coffee hot.”

zeile.text: Always. Leave it with me.

events.lage: At the bottom of the town hall steps a Vespa is waiting with its engine running. Mina isn't grinning, and it makes her look like someone else. On the seat is a bundle of letters tied with a rubber band, three weeks thick.

zeilen.text: You're going up to San Martinu. Don't look at me like that, Yacht, the whole street knows. I go every Thursday, and Nonna gives me cake. But since the animals came I can't get past the bridge.
So take them, please. Some of these are for the brothers, and they'll be wanting them.

optionen.text: Takes the letters. “I'll bring you back some cake.”

zeile.text: You'd better. The chestnut one. Not the lemon, the lemon is a punishment.

events.lage: Lola has been talking about this shop for ten minutes and she still can't find the door. It is behind the harbour, down an alley that smells of drying nets. Inside there are too many shelves for the room: rice, noodles, tins, a wall of amber bottles, a small Virgin Mary with a fresh flower in front of her. At the back a very small old woman in a silk blouse stands over a very big pot. She looks at Lola. Then she looks at you, for a long time. Then she picks up a bowl.

zeilen.text: Auntie! This is my boss, the one from the quay, he cooks too, properly, I told you! I just need two bottles of the good fish sauce, and then I'll get out of your way.
You, later.
Him, now. Sit. Ăn đi. Eat. You are too thin, con. Who let you go out like this?

optionen.text: Takes one bite before he says anything. It's thịt kho, and it tastes like the kitchen at home. “My parents left after the war. Germany, in the end.”

zeile.text: Germany. Cold. Good schools. She did well, your mother. Eat, there is more egg.

optionen.text: Says it in Vietnamese, badly. “Dạ. Con cảm ơn bà.”

zeile.text: This accent. Your mother should be ashamed. Say it again, slowly, and then you can have more.

optionen.text: Looks into the pot. “You put a little too much sugar in the caramel.”

zeile.text: Too much, he says. Sixty years, too much. Good. Now you sit, you tell me how much is right, and then I tell you why you are wrong.

optionen.text: “I'm fine, thank you. I already ate on the boat.”

zeile.text: On the boat. That is not eating. That is fuel. Sit.

Inside there are too many shelves for the room: rice, noodles, tins, a wall of amber bottles, a small Virgin Mary with a fresh flower in front of her. At the back a very small old woman in a silk blouse stands over a very big pot. She looks at you for a long time. Then she picks up a bowl.

events.lage: You are counting out money for rice when the shop door bangs open. Nonna Fiora has come all the way down the mountain, with a wooden spoon in one hand and a green stalk in the other. It is the lemongrass you planted.

zeilen.text: There is grass in my garden. Foreign grass, in my bed, next to my garlic. Did you think I wouldn't see it?
It is not grass. Smell it. In Saigon we put it in everything, and nobody died.
I did smell it. I put it in the soup last night, to show them how bad it is. The whole table asked for more.
Of course they did. You keep good soil up there, Fiora. It never grew like that behind my shop.
And you keep good roots. I want more of them. Come up on Sunday, and I will feed you properly.
You will feed me? I will bring the pot. You are too thin.

optionen.text: Takes a very long time counting his coins, so he can stay and listen.
“So it was good?”

zeile.text: Don't push your luck. Pay for your rice. We are talking.

events.lage: You only came in for rice. She puts the rice on the counter and keeps her hand on it.

zeilen.text: When did you call your mother? I'm not asking when she called you. A mother always calls. I'm asking when you called.

optionen.text: Takes out his phone and rings home, right there at the counter. “Mẹ? It's me. No, nothing's wrong.”

zeile.text: Good. Now you can have the rice. Tell her you are eating. Don't tell her what.

optionen.text: “Last week, I think.”

zeile.text: You think. She knows exactly. To the day, she knows. The rice stays here until you know too.

events.lage: The whole village is standing in the street, and nobody is going in. Over the door of the old shop house opposite Alva's bar hangs a new sign, cold and white even in the sun. You know that logo. You held it in your hand yesterday, on a small black part from your generator. Across the street Alva stands in her doorway with a cloth in her hand, not wiping anything. In the middle of it all a thin young man in a white polo shirt is giving out coupons.

zeilen.text: Free coffee! Opening day, the first one is free, it's really free, you only need the app. No, there's no app yet. Ha. Just take one.
Alex. It says Alex on your chest. Sandru, I have known you since you were eating sand. Who is Alex?
It's for the system, Elsa. The system didn't like the other one.
You're the one from the quay. Hi. Alex. Sandru. Either is fine, really. Coffee?

optionen.text: Takes a coupon and looks up at the logo. “Who owns this place?”

zeile.text: A company in Monaco. They send the prices, and I put them on the shelves. I've never actually met anyone. That's normal, I think?

optionen.text: Looks across the street at Alva. “She doesn't look happy.”

zeile.text: No. It was her mother's house. Sorry, it is her mother's house. I know exactly whose house it is, I carried crates in here when I was twelve.

optionen.text: Hears something small when he steps closer, a thin electric hum. “What's that noise?”

zeile.text: Nothing. New shoes.

optionen.text: Gives the coupon back. “Not today.”

zeile.text: That's okay. Nobody today, so far. You're in very good company.

events.lage: The bar goes quiet when he comes in, the way a bar does. Sandru is still wearing the white shirt, and he walks to the counter carefully, listening to his own legs. Behind Alva hangs her father's chalkboard, with the whole village on it and what each of them orders. His name is still there, low down, in an old man's handwriting. Sandru: orangeade.

zeilen.text: A grappa, please, Alva.
We're out.
You are holding the bottle.
I know what I'm holding. Here.
I'm thirty, Alva.
I know how old you are. I was there. Take that thing off my mother's house, Sandru.
You know I can't.
I know. Drink your orangeade.

optionen.text: Sits down on the next stool. “I'll have what he's having.”

zeile.text: Two orangeades. God help this bar.

optionen.text: Stays at the counter with her. “He looks like he came to say something.”

zeile.text: He did. He has been coming to say it since he was eleven.

optionen.text: Puts money down for both glasses and leaves them to it.

zeile.text: Take that back. Papa never charged for that orangeade, and I'm not going to start.

events.lage: Three days later they hold the service in the monastery garden. There is nothing to bury, so there is a row of folded habits on a long table, with a candle for each one. The deputy mayor arranged all of it: the candles, the chairs carried up the mountain, and the priest, who has shaved and is nearly standing straight. Pascal has taken off his hat. You have never seen him without it. Frederico holds a basket of bread, baked too dark on purpose.

zeilen.text: I did not come up here when the animals came. That is the first thing I have to say here, and I should say it before the other things.
You're late, Anghjulu.
Yes, Fiora.
Pascal. The chairs, the candles. You paid for all of it, don't tell me you didn't. You are a good man.
No, no. Please, Madame. Leave it with me.

optionen.text: Takes the rubber band off Mina's letters and lays each one on the habit it belongs to.

zeile.text: Brother Teo's sister writes every month. She doesn't know yet. I will write to her tonight.

optionen.text: Keeps the letters in his jacket and gives them to Nonna afterwards, without a word.

zeile.text: Later, yes. You were brought up properly. Somebody should tell your mother.

events.lage: Three days later they hold the service in the monastery garden. There is nothing to bury, so there is a row of folded habits on a long table, with a candle for each one. The deputy mayor arranged it all, and the priest has shaved. Nonna comes out last and sits at the back. At the end of the table, past the last habit, somebody has put a wooden goat. It has no candle.

zeilen.text: I did not come up here when the animals came. That is the first thing I have to say here, and I should say it before the other things.
You're late, Anghjulu.
Yes, Fiora.
Nobody told me there was a boy. I ordered for the brothers, I only ordered for the brothers. Please wait. I'll go down and get one more. It's an hour, please don't start without him.

optionen.text: Takes the rubber band off Mina's letters and lays each one on the habit it belongs to.

zeile.text: He used to run down to the bridge for these, so Mina wouldn't have to climb. He kept the stamps.

optionen.text: Gives the letters to Isabelle and waits with her for the candle.

zeile.text: Thank you. It's a long way down. He'll run. Look at him, he's already running.

events.lage: Mina is waiting at the bridge with the engine off. Nonna gave you something for her, in a napkin: a piece of chestnut cake. Mina breaks it in two and gives you the bigger half, and for a while nobody says anything.

zeilen.text: So, Yacht. All those letters I gave you for the brothers. Did they read them?

optionen.text: “No. I put them where they belonged.”

zeile.text: Okay. That's okay. I'll go up on Thursday, same as always. There's still post for Nonna.

optionen.text: “Some of them.”

zeile.text: You're a really bad liar, Yacht. Thanks, though.

events.lage: Mina is waiting at the bridge with the engine off. Nonna gave you something for her, in a napkin: a piece of chestnut cake. Mina breaks it in two and gives you the bigger half, and for a while nobody says anything.

zeilen.text: So, Yacht. All those letters I gave you for the brothers. Did they read them?

optionen.text: “No. I put them where they belonged.”

zeile.text: I'll do the harvest now, in the mornings. Don't say anything, okay? Just don't say anything.

optionen.text: “Some of them.”

events.lage: At the bottom of the drainpipe a round, sun-browned man in a black cassock stands with his sleeves rolled up and a flask in his hand, looking up at the tower with deep satisfaction.

events.lage: Sunday. The bell rings in nearly the right rhythm. Everybody has come, because the church has a new roof and nobody wants to look as if they've noticed. Bà Tư sits in the first pew with a prayer book older than the building. Pascal goes along the rows with the collection plate and says every name. Sandru sits at the back near the door, where it's easier to stand up. Madame Casanova has a card up her sleeve. Alva hasn't come. Mina arrives during the first reading. You can hear the Vespa.

Arcturus, fifty-one and a bit. Polaris, forty-two, which is what it's supposed to be, so we are where we think we are. That's the whole sheet, and I haven't looked at a single card.

events.lage: Past midnight. Sophia has laid out a pack of cards on the table, and she's dealing to you without asking. Her glasses are pushed up in her hair. She loses the first hand, and the second. You've watched her take money from Yamamoto every night for a week.

events.lage: Bibi has one post in the ground and a pile of others, and she waves you over with a hammer. It's the first fence at Mochi's. Whatever it's meant to keep in is already standing on the other side, watching.

Pass me the nails, Clipboard. Not all of them. Why would I need all of them?

You came up here on your day off to help me steal from an ape, Clipboard. I just want you to know that I noticed.

And there's no refund. I'd like that written very clearly. You do numbers, mon chou. It means cabbage, don't look at me, I didn't invent France. Is that the stupidest thing you've ever heard?

zeile.text: You'll regret that. So, this one came with the wrong paperwork –

optionen.text: “Not tonight, I think. I'd like to stay until it wakes up, though.”

zeile.text: Yeah. Yeah, okay. That's a good answer, you know. Nobody ever stays for the waking up.

events.lage: Elsa has asked you to look through the ARK papers, because you read this kind of thing for a living. Bibi is mending a feed sack beside you on the wall. You read out the front of a glossy brochure, the way you'd read it to a client: “Ark. A rescue programme for animals with nowhere else to go.”

zeilen.text: What do you think of it? As a professional, I mean. You've read a lot of these.

optionen.text: “Whoever wrote this was good. That's the best greenwashing I've seen in years.”

events.lage: Bibi has stopped sewing. She looks at the sack and not at you.

zeilen.text: Thank you.

I was twenty-two. I had a notebook with a zoo in it, no fences, and I'd been drawing it since school. I showed it to Julien on our third date. He said it was beautiful, and he asked if he could keep it.
He kept it. That's my sentence. I told you everything, you know, every animal and every name. I didn't tell you that one. So, what do you do with that?

optionen.text: “You wrote it because you meant it. He's the one who sold it.”

zeile.text: I know that. I mean, I don't. Say it again sometime, when I'm not looking at you.

optionen.text: “Show me the notebook. The real one.”

zeile.text: Nobody's seen it since. It's got crayon in it. If you laugh, I'll set Sorry on you.

optionen.text: “Then you're the best copywriter Alon ever had. Let's take it back.”

zeile.text: Ha! Oh, I'd like that. I'd like to see his face. I want to be the first thing he sees.

events.lage: The gates stand open, and the evening is very quiet. Bibi sits down next to you and pushes the field book against your knee. Then she looks somewhere else.

zeilen.text: That's all of them, every page. Well, nearly. Have you looked at the last one? You don't have to look at the last one. Did you know a vulture can digest bones? So that's interesting.

optionen.text: Opens it at the end.

events.lage: It's a page like all the others, with a photo clipped to it: you, in the yard, with mud in your ear. *Name:* Clipboard, Mon lapin, Hase, Mon canard, Mon chou, Bärchen, each one crossed out, and under them, in careful pencil, *Spatz*. *Favourite food:* mine, sadly. *Bites:* only people he likes. *Release:* no. And then, smaller: ...Ask him first.

zeilen.text: I stayed in Marseille for a man once, and this is not that. This place is mine, and it stays mine. And I'm not signing for you. I signed for things before. I'm only asking.

optionen.text: “Ask me, then.”
“You've spelled it wrong. It's only got one bite.”
“I saw that outline weeks ago. I've been trying to walk like it.”

events.lage: She laughs too loud, and then she stops, and for once she doesn't say sorry. She takes the pencil from behind her ear and looks at the page for a long time.

zeilen.text: Spatz. My mother called me that. Now you know everything. This time it's true.

optionen.text: Stays on the wall with her until it's dark.

betroffen.was: is holding a folder against her chest

events.lage: Nobody has gone home. People sit on the church steps and on the edge of the fountain, too tired to talk. Rosi has a laptop on her knees and a cable running up into the dark. Then, all over the square, the phones light up at once.

zeilen.text: There. Got you. ...We have a signal, Officer. It had a very bad password.
Sent. Every photo, every name, straight to the commission. Now we wait.

optionen.text: Takes out his phone.

events.lage: Every phone in the square shows the same video: a white stage, a sunrise on a giant screen, and a man in a black turtleneck. Alon Varenne smiles like a man launching a phone.

zeilen.text: Last night, pirates attacked a small village in Corsica. Our security team was there in forty minutes.
Zero dead. That is what a future without fear looks like.

optionen.text: Keeps watching.

events.lage: For four seconds, Siri's video is the first thing on every screen: the gate, the smoke, Minicu. Then another video slides over it, and that is the one everybody plays. A white stage, a sunrise, and a man in a black turtleneck: Alon Varenne.

zeilen.text: Last night, pirates attacked a small village in Corsica. Our security team was there in forty minutes.
Zero dead. That is what a future without fear looks like.
Some of you have seen other videos tonight. Please be careful. Today, anyone can make a video.

optionen.text: Keeps watching.

events.lage: Across the square the church door is open, and candlelight falls through it onto the stones. Inside, Don is still sitting with Minicu.

zeilen.text: That was mine. It was up for four seconds.
Forty minutes. ...Nobody came in forty minutes. Nobody came at all.

optionen.text: Looks back at the screen.

events.lage: Alon leans a little closer to the camera, and his smile gets warmer.

zeilen.text: And I want to thank our partners at the Eden Group, and one man in particular. Their consultant on the ground.
Duc. Welcome to the team.

optionen.text: Lowers the phone.

events.lage: The square goes quiet. Nobody here knew that their harbour was being sold. One by one, the faces in the blue light turn towards you. Madame Casanova is the last.

zeilen.text: ...Monsieur?

optionen.text: Opens his mouth.

events.lage: Before you can say anything, your phone rings. Megan. It is the first call that has come through since the war council.

zeilen.text: Duc. I've just read the press release. You're in it, and so is my deal. Neither of us was supposed to be. Don't say a word to anyone until I land.

optionen.text: Says nothing. The screen goes dark.

events.lage: A slow day at Alva's bar. Sophia sits at the end of the counter with her little brown notebook. Alva is drying a glass and looking at all the empty chairs.

zeilen.text: My quiet nights are killing me, Sophia. You did theatre in London, didn't you? Come and read something out loud, a story, anything, and I'll sell wine to the people who come to listen.
Alva, darling, I stood at the side of a stage for two years and I never once went on. It's the thing I'm best at.

You've seen the letters, Duc, now that Alva's gone down to the cellar. Fifteen publishers have said no to M. J. Penrose, and that's me, as you know. But not one of them has ever heard the book out loud.
Ten euros says I'd be sick before the first page. So tell me, and please don't be kind. Should I do it?

optionen.text: Puts ten euros on the counter. “I'll take that bet. Three days from now.”

zeile.text: You put money on the bar. Oh, that's low. You know I can't walk away from a bet.

optionen.text: “Would you read the vicar? The one who'd been dead since Tuesday?”

zeile.text: You remember the marmalade. Yes, I suppose I'd have to read the vicar.

optionen.text: “It's your secret. What do you want, Sophia?”

zeile.text: There you go, asking. Nobody ever does. I want to go on, Duc. Only once, just so I know.

events.lage: Sophia turns the notebook over twice, and then she looks down at her uniform.

zeilen.text: But I can't go up there in this, because they'd all ask me for a table. M. J. Penrose has a coat. I've had it in my head for three books, a camel coat from the thirties with a belt. Ask your friend Danzel if such a thing still exists.

optionen.text: Says he'll ask Danzel.

events.lage: You ask Danzel about a camel coat from the thirties, for a friend. He stops pretending to be busy. Totò is across the piazza, eating something, and he comes over when he hears the word coat.

zeilen.text: A camel coat from the thirties, with real wool. No, nobody makes that cloth any more, and what they sell now would be an insult to her. I would need an old one to take apart, very slowly.
There's only one on this coast that I know of. Totò had it in his locker. He wanted a price that made me feel unwell.

Comandante, that coat! It was an English gentleman's, and nine years I kept it safe. Last night I put it on the table, and I lost it to Yamamoto-san. Two to one on me, I gave myself, and I'm still upset.
If you're going to play him, ask Sophia first. She's the only one who beats him.

optionen.text: Sends Sophia a message. “How do you beat Yamamoto?”
“I'll play him tonight. Tell Sophia I said so.”

zeile.text: I'll tell her, Comandante. Two to one against you, and today I am generous.

events.lage: Sophia's message is still on your phone: “he says sorry when his cards are good. thirty years in a bank, poor man. don't you dare tell him”. Yamamoto is sitting alone with a pack of cards, and the coat is folded on the chair beside him. He stands up and bows to you, and then, you are nearly sure, to the coat.

zeilen.text: Officer-san. Very honoured. Three hands, please. If you win two, you take the coat with my respect.

optionen.text: Sits down and cuts the cards.

events.lage: First hand. Yamamoto looks at his cards and his thumb goes to his watch. Sophia wrote: he says sorry when his cards are good.

zeilen.text: So sorry. I am very tired tonight.

optionen.text: Puts in more money.

zeile.text: So sorry, Officer-san. Three queens.

optionen.text: Gives up the hand.

zeile.text: Very wise. I had three queens, and I was so sorry about them.

events.lage: Second hand. Yamamoto looks at his cards. His hands lie flat on the table. Sophia wrote: he says sorry when his cards are good.

zeilen.text: Very interesting. Your turn, please.

optionen.text: Puts in more money.

zeile.text: Very interesting. I have a pair of twos, and now I have nothing.

optionen.text: Gives up the hand.

zeile.text: A pair of twos, Officer-san. You were afraid of a pair of twos.

events.lage: Last hand. Yamamoto smiles at you and doesn't say a word. Then his thumb goes to his watch, the same way it did on the first hand.

zeilen.text: Sophia-san also watches my mouth. Tonight I will say nothing.

optionen.text: Puts in more money.

zeile.text: You should have watched more than my mouth. A full house.

optionen.text: Gives up the hand.

zeile.text: You did not watch my mouth. You watched my hands. Who taught you this?

events.lage: Yamamoto stands up and lifts the coat from the chair with both hands. He holds it out to you, and he bows.

zeilen.text: Very interesting. So sorry. Please tell Sophia-san she owes me a new way to lose.

optionen.text: Takes the coat with both hands, and bows back.

events.lage: Yamamoto squares the pack and looks at the coat for some time. Then he looks at you, and he bows.

zeilen.text: The coat is heavy, Officer-san, and I carry my own luggage. Forty euros, for Totò's feelings.

optionen.text: Pays him forty euros and takes the coat.

events.lage: Danzel has carried his low box out to the good window of Le Théâtre Rouge. Sophia stands on it in the camel coat, with the belt tied, the hat tilted and a pencil behind her ear. He is kneeling at the hem, and for once he isn't performing. Her long hair has gone. You look again, and it's a short, glossy wave, pinned flat on one side.

zeilen.text: Stand still, please. This cloth is eighty years old and it is better than anything I will ever make, so I took it apart slowly and I built it again around you. The left shoulder is new. I don't think you can tell.

Don't stare, darling, it's all still there under the pins. In London I learned to make long hair look short in ninety seconds in the dark, in case somebody fell ill before the second act. Nobody ever did.
Everything I make has a small label inside the collar, with one name on it. I always leave that until last. What do I stitch?
He's asking you as well, Duc, and you've read the letters. Which name should go in the coat?

optionen.text: “M. J. Penrose. She wrote the book, so let her wear the coat.”

zeile.text: Yes. She's braver than I am, and she has nothing to lose. Stitch it, Danzel.

optionen.text: “Sophia Moore. That's the name you want on a book cover, isn't it?”

zeile.text: You don't make things easy, do you? …Stitch it before I change my mind.

optionen.text: “Leave it empty. You'll know when you're standing up there.”

zeile.text: That is the worst thing anyone has ever said to an actress. …Leave it empty, Danzel.

events.lage: The storeroom behind Alva's bar smells of diesel and old lemons. Through the door you can hear chairs and glasses and people talking. Sophia is standing very straight in the camel coat, holding three pages, and the pages are shaking.

zeilen.text: I've got people standing on the piazza, Sophia, and they're asking me to open the windows.
Every chair is gone, Sophia, and I've given Totò a crate.
Six people, Sophia, and one of them is the priest, so I'm counting him twice.
Two years, Duc. Every single night there was a young man with a clipboard who came along the corridor to say it to the others, and he walked straight past me.
I'd like somebody to say it to me, just once. Would you mind?

optionen.text: Opens the door. “You're on, Miss Penrose.”

events.lage: She takes one breath, and the pages stop shaking. She walks past you, and she doesn't look back. She walks to the counter and lays down her pages. Every face in the bar turns to her.

zeilen.text: Good evening. My name is M. J. Penrose. I don't exist, so please don't ask for your money back.

zeilen.text: My name is… My name is Sophia Moore. M. J. Penrose sends her apologies.
The vicar had been dead since Tuesday, which explained the marmalade.

optionen.text: Waits.

events.lage: Nobody laughs. Her voice was too thin, and the back of the room didn't hear the line. A chair creaks. Somebody asks Alva for more wine. The pages have started shaking again, and Sophia looks down at them and can't find her place. Then she looks up, across the whole bar, at you.

zeilen.text: I'm so sorry. I seem to have lost my place. Where was I?

optionen.text: Nods once, and doesn't look away.

zeile.text: Yes. Thank you. I was at the marmalade, wasn't I?

optionen.text: Calls across the room. “The vicar had been dead since Tuesday!”

zeile.text: So he had, darling, thank you. Would anybody else like to read?

optionen.text: Stands still and says nothing.

zeile.text: No. You're quite right. Nobody is coming to help me, and I think that's rather the point of going on.

events.lage: She takes a breath and reads the line again, louder, and this time she makes them wait for the last word. Don Anghjulu laughs so hard that he has to put down his glass. After that, the whole room is hers. You have watched her work a room a hundred times, but she has never done it like this, because she isn't asking anybody for anything.

zeilen.text: Mrs Trelawney from the post office found him in the church that morning, sitting very straight, with a spoon in his hand. She said good morning to him twice, because she had been brought up properly.
A spoon! No priest eats marmalade with a spoon. God sees everything, and this woman knows my profession.
Three people in the village had wanted the vicar dead for years. All three of them brought a cake to his funeral, and all three cakes were very good.
Two to one on the cakes! Comandante, I'm taking bets. Two to one on the lady from the post office!
It's the cook. It's always the one who feeds everybody, because nobody looks at her.
Nobody looked at Mrs Pascoe either, who had made all three cakes. She had been waiting for this funeral since Easter.

optionen.text: Puts five euros on Mrs Pascoe.

zeile.text: Five on the cook! The Comandante reads people. I'm already sorry I asked.

optionen.text: Tells Totò to be quiet, and keeps listening.

zeile.text: Comandante. I'm quiet. Look how quiet I am. It's still two to one.

events.lage: She reads for twenty minutes more. Alva sells no wine at all, because nobody gets up. Near the end of the chapter Sophia slows down, and then she stops in the middle of a page and looks up. She isn't reading now.

zeilen.text: The last train has gone, and… No. Forgive me, that isn't in the book. That's from something else.
That's the end of the chapter, I'm afraid. I'm told it's a good place to stop.
No. You can't stop there. Who killed him? Sit down, eat something, and then read the next part.
God sees everything, but He hasn't told me about the vicar. I would also like to know.
Did you hear that, Duc? She wants to know what happens next. Fifteen letters, and not one of them ever wanted to know that.
Give me that receipt, Auntie Tu. I've got a pen with my own name on it, and I've never had anything to sign.

optionen.text: Stands up and claps with everyone else.
Doesn't clap, and just looks at her until she looks back.

events.lage: Later, at the counter. The crew came ashore for the wine and stayed for the vicar, and now they've got Sophia cornered.

zeilen.text: Eight and a half. No, nine. You've lived next to me for four seasons, and you wrote three books? I want every one of them, and I'm going to be so loud about this.
You always had ink on your chin in the mornings. I thought it was from doing the bills. Did you know that a vicar – no, sorry. I'm just proper proud of you, that's all.

optionen.text: Raises a glass to them.

fakt.text: Sophia read from her detective novel at Alva's bar, in Penrose's camel coat. Now the whole crew and the village know that she writes.

optionen.text: Leaves them to it, and lets them have her for the night.

fakt.text: Sophia read from her detective novel at Alva's bar, in Penrose's camel coat. Now the whole crew and the village know that she writes.

events.lage: Breakfast, the morning after the reading at Alva's bar. Sophia is back in her uniform, with her hair up, and she sits down next to you without being asked.

zeilen.text: You'll want your ten euros, from when you bet me at Alva's that I'd go through with it. But I was sick in her storeroom about a minute before you got there, darling, so strictly speaking I won.
I was sick in Alva's storeroom before the reading, you know, about a minute before you got there. I thought somebody ought to have it in writing.
I never did find out what it's like to go on in that play. I'll tell you what, though, I find I don't mind at all.

optionen.text: Just smiles.

events.lage: The morning after the reading, nobody on the piazza is talking about anything else.

zeilen.text: Comandante, I'm telling everyone that coat was mine. Nobody has to know about the cards.
There's a letter for M. J. Penrose at the post office again. I've been wondering who that was for years, you know. I've only been wondering, of course.
Best quiet night I ever had. Tell her that she drinks free, once.

optionen.text: Says he'll tell her.
“Once? After that crowd?”

zeile.text: Once. I'm grateful, I'm not stupid.

events.lage: Breakfast is not over when Megan calls. She has a paper in her hand, and she does not say good morning.

zeilen.text: Alon saw Lea's coordinates. His drone was over the bay last night. The ultimatum runs out on day twenty-one, and I don't think he plans to wait for a signature.

Eden Intelligence gives him a hundred percent. That means if he came today, we would lose everything. So we have six days to bring that number down. Everybody on your crew has a job now. Find out what they can do.
And gather timber and stone, every piece you can carry. Whatever he breaks, you'll have to mend the next morning, and nobody will sell you wood in a war.

optionen.text: “Six days. Then we start today.”

zeile.text: Good. Don't be heroic. Be useful.

optionen.text: “A hundred percent of what, exactly?”

zeile.text: Of the people he can send. Ask me again on day twenty, and I'll have a better number for you.

events.lage: A seagull has landed on Minicu's head. He has not moved for an hour. Three children and Mina are watching from the harbour wall, and nobody dares to laugh too loud.

zeilen.text: He is sleeping. I wait.

optionen.text: Sits down next to him and waits too.

zeile.text: His name is Kevin. Pascal gave him the name.

optionen.text: Very quietly takes a photo.

zeile.text: Shh.

events.lage: Lola comes down the gangway with a bowl under a tea towel. Minicu is sitting on a bollard, as if he had been waiting for exactly this, and he has.

zeilen.text: Leftovers, mate. Don't tell Chiara, she counts the spoons.
Do your hands hurt? From the knife? All day?
My – what? Nobody's ever... no. A bit. Mostly. Eat your soup, it's getting cold, and so am I, and – just eat it.

optionen.text: Watches them from the gangway.
Sits down on the next bollard.

zeile.text: She cooks every day. Every day. I carry. She cooks.

events.lage: Jana is dragging a suitcase with a broken wheel along the quay and apologises to every bollard she hits. Then a very large hand takes the suitcase off her.

zeilen.text: Sorry – sorry – oh, sorry, I didn't see you, sorry!
Why sorry? You did nothing.
I... nobody ever... Jessas. Thank you. Thank you, sorry. No. Thank you.

optionen.text: Holds the gangway gate open for them.
“He's right, you know.”

zeile.text: Sorry, Sir. ...I mean, yes, Sir. I'll practise.

events.lage: Through the town hall window you see Pascal at his desk with Minicu. Pascal has written one word at the top of a sheet, in careful, upright letters. Minicu copies it underneath, slowly, with the tip of his tongue between his teeth.

zeilen.text: Again, Minicu. Slower. There you go.
M. I. N. I. C. U. That's me.

optionen.text: Knocks on the window and gives a thumbs up.

zeile.text: Don't tell anyone, Duc. He wants to write his own name on Alva's chalkboard one day. Leave it with me.

optionen.text: Walks on before they see you.

events.lage: After Megan hangs up, the printer in the mess starts by itself. It prints one page, and Chiara pins it to the wall next to the coffee machine. Six jobs, in Megan's words. Wood and Stone: Nobody will sell you wood in a war. Start carrying. Arm the Crew: A stewardess with a mop is still a stewardess. Give her something better. The Law: There is one honest uniform on this island. Find out if it still fits. The Red Trio: Three people in red. Find out whose side they're on before they find out yours. The Village: If they won't open their doors for you, they won't open them for anyone. The Bell: A priest, a bell and a bottle. Get him sober for one evening.

zeilen.text: Six jobs. Of course it's six. I'll tick them off myself, and I'll be very strict about it.
Number One. 'A stewardess with a mop.' Mr. Maximum would like to know who Megan means.

optionen.text: Takes the first pen from Chiara.
Reads it twice, then pours a coffee.

events.lage: The whole village is on the square, and nobody knows where to stand. Holm has a radio and a chair, and she has not sat down. Behind her, Unit-01 rolls out of the workshop, and its one eye glows amber instead of red.

zeilen.text: It's only a practice head. Don't you dare dent her.
Hold the line, Minicu. Leave it with me.
Today nobody dies, so today you may make mistakes. Make all of them. The fishermen will play the agents, and Unit-01 will play the robots. I want to see where you are weak.

optionen.text: Takes the map from Holm. “Show me.”
Looks at Pascal at the north barricade. “Who has that side?”

zeile.text: Mine, Officer. Minicu and I have the north. That's all he has to do.

betroffen.was: has brought her the last of the diesel

events.lage: The chairs are up on the tables. Alva stands on a crate in a black suit you have never seen, with one arm behind Papa's chalkboard. Under the prices, in chalk, it says MINICU 11. She doesn't stop when you come in.

zeilen.text: Hold the crate, o figliolu. And before you say anything, Mamá sent this suit for the day I come back to Seville. I never went, so tomorrow it gets to go out at least.
This was Papa's. It was behind that board for forty years. He fired it once, at a man who wouldn't pay for a bottle, and he missed on purpose. The man paid.
I've oiled it every winter since he died. Don't ask me why. You keep a dead man's things working, that's all.

optionen.text: Looks at the shotgun. “Do you know how to use that?”

zeile.text: He taught me on bottles behind the chapel. I always hit the bottle. Ask me how much of the wall went with it. That's my bar you're defending, so don't thank me – just don't miss.

optionen.text: Looks at the chalkboard. “What would he say?”

zeile.text: He'd tell me to put it back and pour. Then he'd stand in the door with it anyway. That's my bar you're defending, so don't thank me – just don't miss.

events.lage: Lieutenant Ferrandi comes up the gangway with a clipboard. You have never seen her dressed like this: a beret, a heavy vest, long black guards on her forearms. She is very pleased about it, and she is working hard to hide that.

zeilen.text: Lieutenant Ferrandi, coast guard. In the event of an armed attack on the commune, section nine requires this post to assist. So I'm assisting. Two men, one patrol boat and me. Sign here.

This is the combat uniform. They issued it to me five years ago, and it has been in my locker ever since, because nothing ever happens in Cala d'Orsu. I tried it on every spring, to check the fit. That's also in the regulations.
TOTÒ, I can see you behind that crate. The diesel can wait until the twenty-second. I've written that down too.

optionen.text: Signs the clipboard. “It suits you, Lieutenant.”

zeile.text: It's regulation. …It does, doesn't it? Tell anybody, and you get a ticket.

optionen.text: Signs the clipboard. “Welcome aboard. Bring the boat.”

zeile.text: Facts, not speeches. I like that. The war council is at eight, First Officer, and I'll be early.

events.lage: The mess table is covered with the map of the bay. Nobody has touched the food. Holm has put a coffee cup on each front.

zeilen.text: Eden Intelligence sees three fronts: the south beach, the scrub in the west, and the sea. This won't be over in a day. You will see tonight's number on your map tomorrow, and it's better than a hundred.

Agents walk, dogs run, robots come over the rail. The pirates want the houses. I've written down who I'd put where, and you can change it. I won't be on the quay. I'll be on the bridge with a radio, and I hate it.
Whatever breaks, we mend in the morning, with the timber and stone Megan told you to gather on day fifteen. So count what you have before you go to bed.

events.titel: What You Are When You're Not
events.lage: The bridge wing, high above the dark water. Chiara is alone out here, with her grandfather's old sextant beside her on the rail. She isn't using it. By day she is the loudest person on the boat. Up here she isn't.

zeilen.text: Sunset: four. Moon: six. The stars are showing off, so I took two points away. I'm rating the sky, Duc, because I've run out of things to count.

Everyone on this boat needs me to know what happens next. I've got a list for tomorrow, and it's a very good list, and I don't know what happens next. I don't want to be the Chief Stewardess for the next few hours. Can you do that? Can you tell me what I am when I'm not?

optionen.text: Takes the sextant out of her hand and puts it down. “Nobody needs anything from you until morning. Come with me.”

szene_intim.hinweis: The night before the fighting, or between two days of it. Chiara has no list tonight and nothing to organise, and she finds that hard, then funny, then not funny at all. She won't say goodbye, and she doesn't talk about tomorrow.

zeile.text: …No list. All right. I'm not telling you the number. It isn't on the scale.

optionen.text: Stands next to her at the rail and says nothing at all.

zeile.text: …Seven. No. Don't talk. Stay like this, it's going up.

optionen.text: “You're the person who stays up to rate the moon. I like her. Tell me about the stars.”

zeile.text: Oh, now you've done it. That one's a four, it thinks it's better than it is. Sit down. This could take a while, and I'm glad.

events.lage: The aft deck, past midnight. Sophia's glasses are pushed up in her hair, and her little brown notebook is lying closed on the table. You have never seen her put it down and walk away from it.

zeilen.text: No cards tonight, I've put them away. It seemed unfair, I'd only have taken your money, and you may need it. I have been meaning to tell you. You've been losing a bet to me since the first week.

I bet you'd ask me what I actually want before the week was out. You did, in your way. So here it is, with no show. I'd like one hour where nobody needs me. Just one. Do you think you could not need me, darling? Is that a terrible thing to ask?

optionen.text: “No. It isn't. I don't need a thing from you, Sophia. Come inside, and we'll waste it.”

szene_intim.hinweis: Sophia asked for one hour in which nobody needs her. Her charm comes off bit by bit, and her sentences get short and plain. She won't talk about tomorrow, and she won't manage him.

zeile.text: …You'd better mean that. Bring nothing. I'm so tired of bringing things.

optionen.text: Pulls a blanket over her shoulders, and for once she lets someone do it.

zeile.text: That's my job, you know. Thank you. I'll be perfectly charming about it at breakfast.

events.lage: The foredeck. Lea is lying on her front with her head over the side, and the water below her shines faintly blue wherever a fish turns. She doesn't look round when you come. She knows your walk by now.

zeilen.text: Look down, look at the water, there. See it? That's plankton, it glows when something moves, it's proper glow. Did you know they do it to frighten off – no. I don't know why they do it. I've forgotten. I never forget.

This is the sign for stay together, two fingers, like this. You make it to your dive buddy, and it means don't go where I can't see you. I know it doesn't work on land. Will you make it back anyway? I just want to see you do it.

optionen.text: Makes the sign, two fingers, and holds out a hand. “Come on. Not where I can't see you.”

szene_intim.hinweis: Lea talks fast until she is alone with him, and then she goes slow and quiet. Two fingers mean stay together. She doesn't want to go fast tonight, and she doesn't want to talk about tomorrow.

zeile.text: Okay. Okay, proper okay. Not fast, though. Is that all right? I don't want to go fast tonight.

optionen.text: Makes the sign and stays until the blue goes out of the water.

zeile.text: There. Now you've said it, and you can't take it back, that's the rule. Dreckly, then. Dreckly, we'll all go and see the wreck.

events.lage: The generator room is warm and it smells of diesel. Rosi sits on a toolbox with a spanner that she doesn't need. On the wall is her board, Rosi versus Officer, every repair and duel since your first day, and she is winning, because she keeps the score.

zeilen.text: Officer. You're in my generator room at this hour, and nothing's broken, so don't pretend it is. I've checked. Twice. The score on my board is very much in my favour, by the way, if you were wondering.

If something happens tomorrow, you'd win by default, and I do not accept that. I've never lost to you, and I'm not losing that way. So you're going to stay here tonight and be alive at me. That's not a question. …All right, it's a question. Will you?

optionen.text: Shuts the door behind him. “It's a draw until the morning. Nobody's keeping score.”

szene_intim.hinweis: The door is shut, and Unit-01 hums behind it. Rosi keeps score out loud because she is afraid, and she is not as sure of herself as she is with machines. She will not say the word goodbye.

zeile.text: Somebody's always keeping score. But I can do it later. This is my destiny, Officer, and if you tell anyone I said that, I'll deny it.

optionen.text: Takes the marker and adds one line to her side of the board.

zeile.text: What was that for? You can't just give me points. …Leave it. Goodnight, Captain. I said Officer. Go to bed.

events.lage: The sun deck. Siri sits with her knees pulled up inside a big old sweater with small stars knitted across it, and it doesn't fit her. There's no tripod and no phone. It's the first time you have ever seen her without something to look into.

zeilen.text: Hi. Sorry. There's no camera, you can check. Yasin thinks I'm asleep, and the chair over there has been very understanding about it. Sorry, I talk to the furniture when I'm frightened.

This is my father's sweater, you've maybe seen it. One star for each winter evening. I've carried it for six years, and I put it on tonight for the first time, because if tonight was the last chance to wear it, I didn't want it to still be in a suitcase. Is that stupid? Can you tell me honestly, if I'm stupid?

optionen.text: “You're not stupid. Come downstairs, and leave Siri Sea up here.”

szene_intim.hinweis: No camera, no Yasin, no captions. Siri asks real questions and apologises too often, and she laughs at herself before anyone else can. He takes it slowly, and she doesn't talk about tomorrow.

zeile.text: She won't mind, she's very professional. Sorry. Can I keep the sweater on, for a bit? Or – I don't know. You can ask me, nobody ever asks me.

optionen.text: Puts an arm round her and looks out at the water, and neither of you takes a picture.

zeile.text: That's the nicest thing that's ever happened to me that nobody saw. Sorry. Sorry, that's just what I think.

events.lage: The galley, with one light on. Lola is barefoot in old shorts, and she's making a cheese toastie for nobody. She burns everything when someone watches, and you are watching. She reaches over, and she doesn't send you out.

zeilen.text: Toastie, Boss? I've burnt two already, because you walked in. It's what I make Nan when she can't sleep. I mean, I would, if she wasn't in Byron Bay. Mostly the cheese.

I ring her every Sunday. She's ninety-one, and she called the coast guard once when I missed one, the actual coast guard. There's no signal now, mate. So I keep thinking, what if Sunday comes and I can't tell her anything? Would you just stay here with me till the pan's cold?

optionen.text: Takes the pan off the heat. “It's cold enough. Come here, Lola.”

szene_intim.hinweis: Lola is loud and warm, and tonight she is frightened that she won't reach Nan on Sunday. She laughs at her own jokes and she loses the ends of her sentences. Nobody shouts at her here. She doesn't talk about tomorrow.

zeile.text: Oi, that's a perfectly good – yeah. Yeah, all right. You're a menace, Boss, and I reckon I'll make you breakfast after. I've heard that's how it goes.

optionen.text: Stays until the pan is cold, as she asked, and washes it for her.

zeile.text: You've done that wrong, you've used soap. Nobody's ever done that wrong for me before. Night, Boss.

events.lage: The quay, very late. The chairs from the bar stand on the stones where somebody left them. Alva has put Papa's shotgun across one of them, and she has a dark dress on that you have never seen. There's nobody else here, and she has been waiting for that.

zeilen.text: No music. Don't look for it, there isn't any. This is my grandmother's dress, and I had it ready for Seville when I was twenty-two. Thirteen years it's been in a cupboard, and I've told everyone in this village that I don't dance any more. Stand over there. Don't clap.

My mother rings every year at the end of the season. When do I get you back, she says. I always say next year, o figliolu. It's a good line, it gets a laugh. Tonight I'd like someone to have seen this, in case next year turns out to be a thing I can't promise.

I don't do goodbyes, I do tabs. So you were never here, and I never danced. Everybody's welcome, nobody's mine, you know how it goes. Now tell me, since you came all the way down here. What are you going to do about it?

optionen.text: “You danced, and I saw it. Come with me, and don't give me a line.”

szene_intim.hinweis: Alva flirts with everybody and belongs to nobody, and tonight she has stopped doing that. There is no speech and no promise. She doesn't do goodbyes, she does tabs, and she will not say the word tomorrow.

zeile.text: No line. Nobody in this village has ever seen me go up a gangway at night. Take me up there, o figliolu, and turn the light off. And in the morning you owe me nothing.

optionen.text: “Dance it once more. I wasn't ready.”

zeile.text: Nobody's ever ready. It's better without the clapping, isn't it? Don't tell them. They'd only want me to do it at the Festa.
